patient_information: A 14-year-old girl from the Solomon Islands.
chief_complaint: Painless, non-healing large ulcer of the left leg for one month.
history_of_present_illness: A 14-year-old girl reported a painless, non-healing large ulcer on her left leg that began one month earlier. A smaller, similar satellite lesion was also noted lower down on the same leg, which is a typical presentation for early yaws lesions. There were no other reported symptoms.
exposure_and_epidemiology: The patient was from the Solomon Islands, a region in the West Pacific where yaws is still a common problem. Yaws is spread by skin-to-skin contact in warm, humid environments and is normally seen in young children.
physical_exam: On examination, there was a large lesion approximately 3 cm in diameter on the left lower leg, covered by a layer of crust. A smaller, similar lesion was noted further down the leg. There was no regional lymphadenopathy or evidence of any other skin or bone lesions.
labs_and_diagnostics: A rapid plasma reagin (RPR) test was positive at a titre of 1:64. The patient was seen again 12 months later, and a repeat RPR test was positive at a titre of 1:8.
differential_diagnosis: The primary diagnosis considered was yaws. Other relevant differential diagnoses included skin lesions caused by Haemophilus ducreyi, pyoderma, tropical ulcer, cutaneous diphtheria, and Aeromonas hydrophila infection.
management_and_clinical_course: The patient was treated with a single intramuscular dose of benzathine benzylpenicillin, and the skin lesion resolved over the next 10 days. She presented again 12 months later with a similar ulcer on the right leg. The repeat RPR titre showed a greater than four-fold fall to 1:8, which was considered evidence of cure from the initial infection. The new ulcer on the other leg was therefore interpreted to be of a different aetiology.
final_diagnosis: The final diagnosis was yaws, a chronic infectious disease caused by Treponema pallidum subspecies pertenue. The diagnosis was based on the clinical findings of a characteristic chronic leg ulcer with a satellite lesion in a patient from an endemic region. The diagnosis was supported by a high-titer positive rapid plasma reagin (RPR) test of 1:64, and confirmed by the lesion's resolution after treatment and a greater than four-fold fall in the RPR titre at follow-up, indicating cure.
